Prescription marijuana legally sold in Dutch pharmacies from Monday

By TOBY STERLING, Associated Press Writer

AMSTERDAM, Netherlands - Just what the doctor ordered?

Starting Monday, pharmacies in the Netherlands are legally authorized to fill prescriptions for marijuana as a medicine.

In practice, some Dutch doctors have recommended marijuana for years, mostly to cancer patients as an appetite enhancer and to combat pain and nausea. But it was usually bought at one of the country's 800 " coffee shops, " where small amounts of the weed are sold openly while police look the other way.
(MarijuanaNews note: Actually, the police don't really look the other way. ". Dutch police are free to patronize coffee shops when they are off duty.)

A bill authorizing pharmacies to fill marijuana prescriptions was approved by a large majority in the Dutch parliament in 2001, and went into effect Monday. It also allows patients to apply for refunds from their medical insurance, but not all policies cover weed.

Bas Kuik, a spokesman for the Dutch Ministry of Health, said the point of the law was to ensure that patients have access to a supply containing consistent levels of tetrahydrocannabinol, or " THC, " the primary substance active in marijuana.

" The health minister said, look, doctors are prescribing marijuana to their patients anyway, and there are many medicinal users, so we may as well regulate it, " he said.

The Dutch government's stance is in stark contrast to U.S. federal law, which says growers of marijuana for medicinal purposes face the same prison terms that recreational growers do.

Kuik said that that the Dutch government will license several official growers later this year. Meanwhile, pharmacies will be left to themselves to decide how to fill prescriptions.

Many pharmacies use marijuana packaged by Maripharm, a company that advertises its product as " standardized, vacuum-packed and bearing patient information and dose advice. "
(MarijuanaNews note: Click on the Maripharm link for an interesting background in English.)

Laura Sluisen, who works at the Dam Pharmacy on Amsterdam's central square, said Maripharm marijuana has been available there for a long time, but few people buy it.

" I have to say that it actually almost never happens in practice, " she said.
(MarijuanaNews note: Although I have reported it on MarijuanaNews, this is the first article that I have seen that confirms that a few Dutch pharmacies never stopped providing medical cannabis.

There are two reasons that so few people went to pharmacies to get their medical cannabis.

First, it was not covered by insurance. Now there is an economic incentive.

Second, the Mediwiet program started in 1996 by Dutch cannabis pioneer Wernard Bruining and Nol van Schaik of Haarlem made cannabis available to patients at a 50% discount in participating coffee shops. This meant that it was cheaper in coffee shops and they had a greater variety.)

Prices for marijuana in coffee shops range from 2 euros to 16 euros per gram (US$2 to US$16 per 0.04 ounce), depending mostly on the quality and its concentration of THC. Maripharm's product at the Dam Pharmacy costs about 9 euros per gram (US $9 per 0.04 ounce).

Pharmacies typically leave it up to patients whether they want to smoke the weed or make tea from it, but Kuik said smoke-free " inhalers " also are under development.
(MarijuanaNews note: This is probably a reference to vaporizers, not to GW Pharmaceuticals liquids.

To my amazement TechTV, the cable techie news channel owned by Paul Allen recently reported on a high-tech vaporizer called Vapir.)

Recent studies show a fractional increase in the number of people in the Netherlands who say they have tried marijuana, while overall use levels remain well below those in the United States, despite its widespread availability here.
(MarijuanaNews note: One almost never sees this fact reported in the DEAland media.)

However, the percentage of THC in Dutch marijuana has increased sharply in the past several years. A government-sponsored study released this month estimated average THC content at around 15 percent, compared with 6.6 percent in imported marijuana.
(MarijuanaNews note: This is the only fact in this article that we are likely to see mentioned by the prohibitionists. It is an interesting factoid in that it indicates a more rapid increase in THC levels than one might expect. According the TrimbosInstitute in Utrecht the THC content in Dutch nederwiet averaged 11.3 per cent in 2000, compared to 8.6 per cent in 1996. Remember the Dutch market is still contraband at the wholesale level, and such markets place a premium on potency by weight.

Now for an interesting insight into journalism.

News articles are written in what is called the inverted pyramid style. That means that the most important facts are at the top and the least important are at the end, where they are most likely to be cut.

There were two versions of this story on the AP wire. The above version with the factoid about THC levels at the end, where it was likely to be cut, was the first version put out by the AP last night.

A second version was put out this morning with the data on Dutch use levels being below DEAland's at the end, where is likely to be cut. This second version is the one on the New York Times website, but apparently not in the paper. Of course, the Washington Post website doesn't report it at all.)
